activity: Through what Romy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Romy sat on the school rug. Miss Bell held up a big red book. "The words tell me what to say," said Miss Bell. She turned page one first. Then page two. The pages went front to back.

Romy looked at the pages. Little black marks sat in rows. The marks were words. The words told about a tree. On one page, a man put a seed in the ground. On the next page, he helped plant small flowers near it. The story only worked because Miss Bell turned the pages the right way.

After school, the class walked to the library next door. Romy found the tree book. She hugged it to her chest. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

The librarian smiled. She was kind. She put the book in Romy's hands. "You can take it home," she said. "Then bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Romy took the book home. She read it to her teddy bear. Page one first. Page two next. Front to back, just like Miss Bell.

On Friday, Romy put the book in her bag. She carried it back to the library. She set it on the desk. "Here it is," she said. "Now Sam can have a turn."

The librarian put a green stamp on a card. Romy watched the words on the card. The words said Romy's name. Words could do that too.

She skipped back to school, past the tall tree in the yard.

activity: Claire is learning to play a musical instrument.
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Claire went to Miss Rosa's music studio. There was a big violin on a soft chair. Miss Rosa said, "This is for you today." The violin was shiny wood. Claire touched it. The wood felt smooth.

Miss Rosa gave Claire the bow. Claire pulled it across the strings. No sound came out. She tried again. Still no sound. "Why is it so quiet?" Claire asked. Miss Rosa said, "Let's find out." She gave Claire a small orange cake. It was called rosin. "Rub the bow on it, slow and gentle," she said.

Claire rubbed the bow on the rosin. The rosin made little dust, like sand that could color your fingers. Then Claire pulled the bow across the strings. A big sound rang out. "The rosin made it sing!" Claire said. Miss Rosa smiled and clapped. Claire played one more note, slow and long.

activity: Through what Lucy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Lucy sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big spoon. It was too far away.

"Help, please," said Lucy. "I want the spoon."

Dad reached over. He put the spoon by her plate.

"Thank you," said Lucy.

She scooped up her thick potato soup. Yum! Then her elbow bumped her cup. Milk went everywhere. A big white puddle on the table.

Lucy felt her face go hot. "Sorry," she said quietly. "I did not mean it."

"That is okay," said Mom. "We all spill sometimes."

Mom got a towel. She wiped the milk up. The table was dry again.

Lucy kept eating her soup. Then she heard a little sound. Drip, drip. A worm of soup ran down her chin!

"Lucy, your chin is dripping," said Dad.

Lucy laughed. She got her napkin. She wiped her own chin.

"All clean," said Lucy. "I did it myself!"

"Good job," said Mom. She gave Lucy a kiss on her head.

"More soup, please," said Lucy. Dad filled her bowl again.

"Thank you," said Lucy.

She smiled a big, warm smile.

activity: Mya is learning something new. What Mya is learning: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour.
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Mya had three paint pots in the backyard. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. She said it two more times. "Red, yellow, blue."

Mya wanted to paint a flower. But her flower was a purple flower. She looked in her pots. There was no purple paint. She looked again. Still no purple. Her shoulders went down, down, down.

Then she dripped some red on a big rock. She dripped some blue next to it. She mixed them with her brush. Round and round the brush went. The red and the blue made a new colour. The new colour was purple!

Mya hopped up and down. She painted her flower. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. "And purple too!" The purple flower shone in the soft night light.

activity: Charlie is going to the dentist for the first time.
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Charlie put on his red hat. He was not late. The bus came fast!

"Bus, bus!" said Charlie. He held Mama's hand. The big doors opened. They sat by the window. Rain began to fall. The wipers went sweep, sweep across the glass. "Look, Mama! The rain makes them go!"

"We get off at the next stop," said Mama. "The dentist will count your teeth."

They were not late at all. The dentist had a big chair. It went up, up, up! Charlie sat in it.

"Open your mouth wide," said the dentist. Charlie opened it very wide, like a hippo. The dentist counted, "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

"Mama!" said Charlie. "I opened big, so she saw every tooth!"

activity: Lillian is getting a first haircut at a salon.
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Lillian sat in a big chair at the salon. The chair was too tall, so Mommy lifted her up. The hairdresser, Rosa, put a cape around her. "First we brush," said Rosa. The brush went round and round. It made a circle in Lillian's hair.

Rosa picked up her scissors. "Snip," they went. A piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. Lillian looked at it. "How did it fall?" she asked. Rosa snipped again, slow and easy. Another piece fell. "The scissors cut it," said Lillian. "I see it happen." Rosa smiled and kept cutting, bit by bit.

Lillian watched in the mirror. Her long hair was getting short. She liked to wish for short hair like Rosa. Now her wish was coming true, snip by snip. Soon the cape was covered with little hairs. "Where is my ponytail?" Lillian asked. Rosa held it up. "Here it is," she said. Lillian touched one missing spot near her ear and giggled. "All gone," she said. "Snip, snip."

activity: Through what Iris sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread. It was far away. She stood on her chair and reached. Her elbow hit her cup. Milk ran across the table like a little river.

Iris froze. "Oh no," she said. Mama helped wipe the milk. "I'm sorry," said Iris. Mama smiled. "Thank you for saying sorry," she said.

Iris still wanted the bread. This time she folded her hands. "Please pass the bread," she said. Papa put the basket in her hands. "Thank you," said Iris. Papa nodded.

Iris tried to cut her bread. The knife felt too big. Her cut was low and crooked. "This is hard," she said. "Can you help me, please?" Papa put his hand over her hand. Together they cut a neat slice.

Iris took a bite. "The milk spilled because I reached too far," she said. "But I got the bread because I asked." Mama laughed and patted her head. Papa raised his cup. "To asking," he said. Iris raised her cup too, nice and slow.

activity: Through what Sarah sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Sarah wanted to build a tower. She had blocks of many shapes.

"Look, a circle, a square, a triangle," she said. She put a round block on the rug. It rolled away! "Oh no," said Sarah. Why did it roll?

She tried the square block next. The square had flat sides. It sat still. Then she stacked a triangle. It sat still too, on its flat bottom.

"One square, two squares, three squares," she counted. The tower grew tall.

The sun came in the window. It made a shadow on the rug. "Look, my tower has a shadow!" said Sarah. The shadow was tall too.

Mama let her put one more block on top. It was a rectangle, long and flat. The tower stood and stood.

"Round blocks roll. Flat blocks stay," said Sarah. She clapped her hands.

activity: Through what Blake sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Blake wanted the round red ball. Her friend Sam had it. Sam rolled it under the chair. "My turn," said Blake. Sam held the ball tight.

Teacher Mia knelt down. "Let's shake the sand timer," she said. The sand fell down, bit by bit. "When the sand stops, it is a new turn." Sam watched the sand. Blake watched it too.

The sand stopped. Sam gave Blake the ball. He did not cry. He waited. Blake rolled the ball to the wall. The wall pushed it back. "The ball came back to me!" she said. She laughed. The timer turned again. "Sam's turn now," said Blake. She put the ball in his hands. Sam smiled big. "The sand told us when," said Blake. They sat side by side and watched the sand fall.

activity: Through what Amira sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Amira was at Grandma's house. She wanted to make a picture for Grandpa. But she could not find the crayons.

She looked under the big chair. She saw a red sock. She looked behind the small table. She saw a blue cup. No crayons anywhere.

"Did you forget where you put them?" Grandma asked. "Maybe," said Amira. They looked together. Grandma opened a drawer. Inside was a yellow box. It rattled. Amira opened it. The crayons were there!

She sat down to draw. She drew a green frog on red paper. The red paper made the frog look funny. She tried again on white paper. Now the green frog looked bright and good.

Grandma helped her put glue on the back. They stuck the picture on the fridge. Grandpa came in. He touched the frog. "My favorite color," he said. "Green, just like my garden." Amira smiled and drew one more frog, a small one, for his pocket.

activity: Samuel is learning something new. What Samuel is learning: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves.
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Samuel wanted to go outside. The snow was falling. He pulled his red coat off the hook.

He put one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat was on. Now came the tricky part. The zipper.

Samuel pulled the zipper up. It went up a little. Then it stopped. He pulled again. It would not move. The rough zipper tab slipped out of his small fingers.

"Ow," said Samuel. His hand did not bump anything. The zipper was just stuck.

He looked down at the bottom of the coat. There was a little silver pin. It was not inside the little silver box. The pin was outside, all alone.

Samuel pushed the pin into the box. He heard a small click.

"Now I try again," he said.

He pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up. It went all the way to his chin.

"Mom! Look!" said Samuel. "The pin goes in the box. Then the zipper works."

Mom clapped her hands. Samuel ran to the door. The snow was still falling. He pushed the door open and stepped outside.

"Snow!" he shouted.

activity: Olivia is learning to swim at the local pool.
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Olivia went to the pool with Grandpa. She held his hand at the gate. The water was blue and shiny.

"Can I swim today?" she asked.

"Let's try," said Grandpa.

Olivia sat on the pool step. The water was cool on her toes. She kicked her legs. Little waves went up and up. Ooh, the water moved! She kicked again. The waves got bigger. Where would they go?

Grandpa put his arms under her tummy. "Kick and pull," he said. Olivia kicked. She pulled her arms like a puppy. Splash, splash, splash. She moved forward! The kicking made her go.

Then Olivia stopped kicking. She did not go forward anymore. Her feet went down, down, down. Grandpa held her up.

"Sorry, Grandpa! I stopped," she said.

"That's okay. Try again," he said.

So she kicked again. Kick, kick, kick. And she moved through the water, all by herself.

Then something touched her hand. A little rubber duck bobbed by. It floated on the waves she made.

"Grandpa, look! My waves moved the duck!"

"Bring it here," Grandpa said with a smile.

Olivia kicked toward the duck. Her waves pushed it closer. She grabbed it and hugged it.

"Were you swimming too?" she asked the duck. "Quack," said Grandpa.

Olivia laughed so hard that water went up her nose. The duck bobbed on her head.

activity: Charles is searching for a lost favorite toy.
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Charles had a little red car. It was his favorite toy. He brought it to daycare. But now it was gone.

Charles looked under the table. He looked in the doll house. No red car. Miss Ana came to help. She smiled at him. "Let's look together," she said.

Charles looked at the big toy box. It was very full. He pulled out a soft bear. He pulled out some blocks. Then he pushed the box a little. The box tilted. All the toys shifted. Out rolled the little red car!

"My car!" said Charles. He hugged it tight.

Miss Ana gave him a cup of milk. Charles sat down. He held his car in one hand. He drank his milk with the other hand. The young children played all around him. Charles made his car go vroom on the floor. Vroom, vroom, all the way to the snack table.

activity: Through what Charlie sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Charlie wanted to find something yummy for lunch. She looked with her eyes. She saw red tomatoes in the garden. She heard a bee buzz with her ears. She smelled the tomatoes with her nose. "Mmm, they smell good," she said. But how would they taste?

Charlie touched a tomato with her hands. It felt smooth and warm. She picked one and ran to Dad. "Can we eat this?" she asked. Dad washed the tomato at the sink. He cut it into small pieces with a safe knife.

Charlie put a piece in her mouth. She tasted sweet juice. "Yum!" she said. A drop of juice fell on the ground. Soon a little ant came to the drop. The ant drank the juice too. Charlie watched with her big eyes. "Dad, the ant likes it too!" she said. Dad laughed and gave her one more piece.

activity: Through what Myles sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting.
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Myles sat at the dinner table. He wanted more peas. Mom put one pea on his plate. Then she put one more.

"Watch," said Mom. "One, two, three." Three peas sat on his plate. Myles tapped each pea with his spoon. "One, two, three," he said.

Mom slid more peas over. "Four, five, six." Now there were six. Myles counted them too. "Four, five, six!" His voice went up and down like a song.

Dad leaned over. "Can you do seven?" He added one pea. "Seven," said Myles. Dad added more. "Eight, nine, ten." Ten peas! The pile looked big and friendly.

Myles clapped his hands. Then he ate one pea. "Ten went to nine!" said Dad. Myles ate another. "Nine to eight!" Myles laughed and kept eating, counting down with every bite, until his plate was clean.

activity: Harper is getting through an evening power cut at home.
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. Harper looked up from her blocks. The kitchen was dark. The backyard was dark too.

Harper wanted to see her blocks again. "Mama, I can't see," she said. Mama found a big flashlight. She clicked it on. The flashlight made a bright circle on the floor.

Mama pointed the light at the wall. Then she pointed it at Harper's blocks. Harper picked up a red block. She held it near the light. Now the block had light on it. She held it in the dark. The block went dark too. She held it near the light again. It was bright again.

"I can make it light!" Harper said. She moved her teddy bear near the light. The teddy's white tooth showed bright. She moved the teddy away. The tooth was hard to see.

Papa came out with bread and cheese. "We can't bake tonight," he said. "The oven is off." So they had a picnic on the blanket instead.

Harper moved her cup near the light. She moved her plate near the light. She made each thing glow. Mama held the flashlight steady and waited. The wind blew outside. Harper lay back on the blanket and looked up.

The stars were out. "Look, Mama," said Harper. "The sky has its own big light."

activity: Through what Jake sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Jake went to the store with Mom. He saw a big box of cookies. "Can we buy them?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "We can buy them later."

Jake felt sad. "I want them now," he said. Mom said, "We bought apples yesterday. Do you remember? Today we need milk. Tomorrow we can come back for cookies."

Jake thought hard. Yesterday was the day already gone. Today was this day. Tomorrow was the next day. So cookies came after one sleep.

Jake helped Mom find the milk first. He put it in the cart. Then he saw the cookie box again. "Tomorrow," he told himself. He patted the box softly.

At home, Jake put the milk in the kitchen. "Mom," he said, "I love cookies. I will wait for tomorrow." Mom smiled and hugged him.

The next morning, Jake woke up early. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "It is today now. Yesterday was the waiting day." They went back to the store. Jake held the cookie box all the way to the kitchen. He ate one cookie and said, "Waiting made the cookie day come!"

activity: Through what Isla sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Isla wants to paint a cat at daycare. She paints one ear. She paints the other ear. She paints a long orange tail. "Now I can take it home," she says. But Miss Jo touches the paper. "It is still wet," she says. "The paint is slow. It needs time." Isla feels sad. She wants the cat now. She puts her painting on the shelf to dry. Then she plays with blocks. Later, after snack, she touches the paper. The paint is dry now. But Miss Jo says, "We send paintings home tomorrow, not today." So tomorrow comes, and Isla holds her cat all the way to the car. In her bag there is one more surprise. A tiny painted cat from her friend Tom. "He made it for me yesterday," she laughs. "Yesterday, and today, and tomorrow too!"

activity: Jasper is cooking or baking a meal for the family.
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Jasper woke up in the big tent. The birds were singing outside. He wanted to make breakfast for Mom and Dad. He took his toy elephant out to the picnic table. "You can sit here and watch," he said.

Dad helped him light the little camp stove. Jasper poured pancake batter into the pan. The batter went into a round circle. Then he waited. But soon, smoke came up. The pancake turned brown and black. It smelled bad.

Jasper looked at the stove. The middle part glowed very red. "The fire is too hot," he said. "Too hot makes it burn." He slid the pan to the side of the stove. The side was not so red and not so hot.

He poured a new pancake in the pan. It sat on the low heat. It bubbled slowly. Little holes popped on top. Jasper flipped it over with a spatula. The pancake was gold, not black.

Mom and Dad woke up. They sat at the table. Jasper gave each of them a warm plate. Dad ate three pancakes. Mom ate two. The toy elephant sat by the syrup. Soon everyone was full and slow and almost asleep in the sunny morning. "More pancakes tomorrow," said Jasper.

activity: Harrison is celebrating a birthday with family and friends.
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Harrison ran into Grandma's kitchen. "Is the cake ready?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "Almost! We put candles on it now."

The cake was big and pink. Grandma put on one candle. Then two. Then three. "Why three?" asked Harrison. "You are three years old today," said Grandma. "One candle for each year."

Harrison counted them out loud. "One, two, three! I am three!"

Then everyone came in. Mom, Dad, Grandpa, and his cousins too. They made a team around the table. They sang the birthday song, loud and happy.

"Now blow!" said Grandpa. "If you leave the candles lit, the wax will drip on the cake. That would be mean to the cake!"

Harrison took a big breath. He blew hard. Out went one candle. Out went two. But the third one stayed lit! Harrison laughed and blew again. Out it went.

Then Grandma said, "Look, one more surprise!" She pulled out a tiny present from her pocket. It was a little toy truck. "Happy birthday, Harrison."

Harrison held it up high. "Best cake day ever!"

activity: Mohamed is learning something new. What Mohamed is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Mohamed ran to the kitchen in his pajamas. "Today I make my own breakfast!" he said. Mama smiled and put warm toast on a plate.

Mohamed took the butter knife. He pushed hard on the toast. The toast ripped into two pieces. "Oh no," said Mohamed. He looked at the butter. It was cold and hard from the fridge. Then he saw Mama's toast sitting near the warm stove. He held his knife near the stove for a minute, then scooped a little butter. The butter was soft now. It spread easy, like paint on paper. "The warm knife is the answer!" he said.

Next came the milk. Mohamed held the jug far above the cup. Milk splashed on the table. He tried again. This time he kept the jug close to the cup. The milk went right in. Not one drop spilled.

Mohamed sat down and took a big bite. "Mama, come look!" he shouted. "My toast is whole. My cup is full. And the table is dry!" He lifted his cup high like a king.

activity: Through what Mason sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Mason stood by the snack table. He wanted the warm muffin. But it was up too high. He could not reach it.

Miss Amy said, "Use your nose, Mason!" Mason sniffed with his nose. Mmm, the muffin smelled sweet. "I smell it with my nose!" he said. Bella giggled. "I hear Miss Amy with my ears." Then she heard the timer beep. Beep, beep!

Miss Amy gave Mason a short muffin, just his size. He touched it with his fingers. Warm and soft. He took a little bite. "I taste it with my tongue!" he said. Bella clapped. "Ears, nose, fingers, tongue," she counted. "And eyes!" said Mason. He looked at his plate. It was empty. He had eaten it all. "More muffin, please!" said Mason.

activity: Through what Jasper sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the days of the week, the months and the idea that a calendar shows when things happen.
knowledge_domain: the days of the week, the months and the idea that a calendar shows when things happen
story:
Jasper brought his helmet to school. Today was Bike Day, he was sure. He wanted to wear his helmet all day. "Not yet," said Miss Pim. "Bike Day is Friday."

Jasper frowned. "Today is Friday!" Miss Pim pointed at the calendar. "Look. Each box is one day. Today is Tuesday. We have three more days to go." Jasper put his finger on Tuesday. He slid it to Wednesday. Then Thursday. Then Friday. "The calendar says Friday is here," he said. "When I get to the last box, it is bike time!"

Milo laughed. "You touched Friday with your finger. Now it will come faster." Jasper slid his finger back and forth, fast, fast, fast. "Zoom! I am riding my finger like a bike!"

On Friday, Miss Pim turned the page. A new month showed. "October is done," she said. Jasper looked at the page. It said November. He slid his finger to the red box. "Friday," he said. "The calendar knew it all along." His helmet was in his bag, sharp and shiny. The wheels went round and round.

activity: Through what Milo sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow.
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Milo went to the park with Dad. The sun was very hot. Milo had a small ice pop. "It will melt fast," said Milo. He ran to the big tree and sat in its shade. The bark felt rough on his hands. The shade was cool and dark.

A big dog walked by. It went very slow. Then a small dog ran by. It went very fast. "The little one has little legs," said Milo. "Little legs go fast fast fast." Dad laughed.

But the ice pop was dripping. Drip, drip, onto Milo's shoe. The sun came out from behind a leaf. "The sun makes it melt," said Milo. "I need more shade." He put his cap on the ice pop. The cap did cover it, but not all of it.

Then Dad had a big idea. He tipped his own big hat over the ice pop. Now all of it was in shade. The ice pop stopped dripping. Milo ate it up. "Cold and sweet," he said. "Let's take the slow way home, so I can look for more dogs." A ladybug landed on Dad's big hat. "Hello," said Milo.

activity: Theo is learning something new. What Theo is learning: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes.
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Theo sat at the little red table. Miss Maple held up a big card. "This is T," she said. "T goes tuh, tuh." Theo looked down at his shoes. All the letters looked like squiggles to him.

Then Miss Maple said, "Look at your name, Theo." She wrote it on the board. T, H, E, O. Theo pointed at the first letter. "Hey! That is the T card letter!" he said. "That one goes tuh." Miss Maple smiled. "Yes. T is for Theo."

After snack, the ice pop in Theo's bowl began to melt. He watched the sweet pink juice run down to the bottom. "My tongue is cold," he said. Miss Maple laughed. "Cold starts with C," she said. Theo closed his eyes and thought hard. "C is in cold. T is in Theo. The letters are in the words!"

At play time, Theo found letters everywhere. He found an O in his sandwich bite. He found an M in the toy train tracks. He ran to Miss Maple. "I found a letter on the floor!" he said. It was a paper H. "H goes huh," said Theo. "H is in Theo too." He held the letter all the way home.

activity: Maria is making an art or craft project.
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Maria went to the art studio with her dad. She wanted to make a big painting for her grandma. On the door there was a sign. It said "Paint Day!" Maria clapped her hands.

First she painted a red cat. Then she painted one blue shoe, two blue shoes, three blue shoes. But the shoes looked funny. The paint was so wet that the blue ran down into the red cat. Now her cat had blue feet. Maria laughed. "Silly cat!"

She painted a yellow sun next. She tipped the paper up to see it better. The yellow paint slid down and made long stripes. "Look, Dad! My sun has rain!" Maria tipped the paper again and again. Stripe, stripe, stripe. "My cat has rain too," she said, and giggled. "A rainy cat day for Grandma!"

activity: Through what Ethan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Ethan was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to play with the furry gray cat. But his cousin Mia wanted to hold the cat too.

"Me first," said Ethan. He grabbed the cat. The cat jumped down and ran under the chair. Now nobody had the cat.

Grandpa had an idea. He held up a shiny coin. "Heads, Ethan goes first," he said. He flipped it. The coin landed on heads.

Ethan petted the cat very gently. The cat purred. Then Ethan counted to ten, like Grandpa taught him. He passed the cat to Mia. Mia let the cat lick her hand. Then she passed him back.

The cat stayed on their laps all afternoon. "Two turns, one cat," said Grandpa. Ethan smiled and patted the cat's soft head one more time.

activity: Through what Audrey sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Audrey sat in her car seat. She was hungry and wanted a snack. "Daddy, do you have any food?" she asked.

Daddy reached back with one hand. "Look in the bag," he said. Audrey looked in the bag. She found an apple, some crackers, and a banana. The apple rolled when the car turned. The crackers did not roll. The banana stayed still too. "The apple is a round one," Audrey said. "It rolls!" She held it with gentle hands so it would not roll away.

Audrey ate her crackers. Then she saw a cow in a field. "Moo!" she said. Next she saw a dog by the road. Then she saw ducks in a pond. "So many animals," she said.

Soon Audrey got sleepy. "Can I take a nap?" she asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "I will wake you at home." Audrey hugged her toy bunny close. The car went hum, hum, hum. Her eyes closed slowly.

Daddy parked the car. He picked her up, bunny and all. "Time to come in," he whispered. Audrey smiled in her sleep.

activity: Through what Dylan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed.
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Dylan sat at the dinner table. He saw rice and beans and carrots. But Dylan wanted cake.

"I want cake now," said Dylan.

Mom said, "First we eat dinner. Then we can have cake."

Dylan pushed his plate away. His tummy made a little growl. Grrr. It was not full yet.

Dylan looked at Dad. Dad ate his rice, one bite at a time. Dad was slow and calm. Dylan waited and watched.

Then Dylan picked up his spoon. He took one bite. Then another. He ate the beans. He ate the carrots. His tummy felt warm and full.

"My tummy is happy," said Dylan.

"Now the cake," said Mom.

Dylan ate the sweet cake too. After dinner, Dad gave him a warm bath. Dylan got all soapy. Then Dad helped him get dry with a big towel. He put on his soft pajamas.

Dylan yawned. A full tummy and warm pajamas made him sleepy.

"We live in a cozy house," said Dylan. "Can we do this again tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Mom. "Every day."

Dylan smiled and climbed into bed.

activity: Dylan is cooking or baking a meal for the family.
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Dylan wanted to make pancakes for his family. But the bowl was high up on a shelf. He could not reach it.

"Too high," said Dylan.

Dad got the bowl down. "Big job, little cook," he said.

Dylan cracked the eggs. A bit of shell fell in. He scooped it out with a spoon. "Got you," he said.

Then Dylan stirred the batter. He stirred and stirred. The lumps went away. The batter became smooth. "Look, Dad! Stirring makes it smooth!"

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Dylan watched from his safe spot.

Dylan set the table. He put out forks and plates. "I am a brave waiter," he said.

Mom took a big bite. "Mmm. Best pancake ever," she said.

Dylan grinned. Then he looked at his plate. His pancake had two eyes and a smile. "Dad! Did you do this?"

Dad winked. "A happy pancake for a happy cook."

activity: Through what Ivy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Ivy wanted her yellow boots. Where were they? "You wore them yesterday," said Mom. Yesterday. That was the day before this day.

Today Ivy had played in the rain. Today was almost done now. The sky outside was dark. When the sky turns dark, it is time for bed.

"I want my boots now," said Ivy. "Boots are for tomorrow," said Mom. "You can wear them later, when the sun comes back."

Ivy looked out the window. The moon made a little slide of light on her floor. She reached out her toes to touch it. The light looked cool and soft.

"Will the moon be here tomorrow too?" she asked. "The moon comes back every night," said Mom. "Sleep now. Boots come later."

Iivy snuggled under her blanket. First sleep. Then sun. Then boots.

"Goodnight, moon," she whispered. "See you tomorrow."

activity: Through what Wren sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Wren went to the store with Dad. She wanted a book about trucks. A new book cost a lot of money. "Not today," said Dad.

Then Wren saw big words on a door. "What does that say?" she asked. Dad said, "It says Library." The words told them what was inside! Wren held her book up. "I open the front first," she said. "Then I read page by page to the back."

Inside, a nice lady let Wren take a truck book home. "Can I keep it forever and ever?" Wren asked. "No," said Dad. "We bring it back on the day the card says. Then other kids can read it too."

At home, Wren hugged the book. "You come home with me," she said. "Then you go back. Books are silly like that." Dad laughed. "Read to me," said Wren. So Dad read the front page first.

activity: Through what Hazel sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Hazel sat in her car seat. She held her fuzzy blanket close. "Are we going on the boat today?" she asked. "Not today," said Daddy. "Today we drive to Grandma's house. The boat comes tomorrow." "I want the boat now," said Hazel. "Now we are in the car," said Daddy. "The boat is later. Later comes after today." Hazel looked out the window. The sun was up. She heard the wheels go hum, hum, hum on the road. She saw a big red truck. "Yesterday I played in the sand," she said. "Today I ride in the car." "Yes," said Daddy. "And after sleep, it will be tomorrow. Tomorrow is boat day." Hazel yawned a little yawn. She hugged her fuzzy blanket. "Sleep comes first," she said. "Then the boat comes after." She closed her eyes. Daddy drove on, quiet and slow. Soon Grandma's front door came into view. "Wake up, Hazel," Daddy said softly. "We are here now."

activity: Miles is starting the first day of school.
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Miles stood at the school gate. His hand held Dad's hand very tight. He did not want to let go.

A boy came up to the gate. He waved his hand. Miles waved back. The boy smiled. Miles smiled too. Dad let go of Miles's hand. Miles waved again, and the boy came closer.

"I have a crayon," said the boy. He held out a red crayon. Miles took it. He drew a big sun on the paper the boy had. The boy drew a cloud. Together they drew a house.

The bell rang. The gate opened. The boy took Miles's hand. "Come on," he said. "Let's go meet Teacher." Miles looked back at Dad. Dad gave him a thumbs up. Miles walked in with his new friend, still holding the red crayon. "That's a special crayon," said the boy.

activity: Through what Romy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Romy's class walked to the school library. It smelled like paper and rain. The shelves were tall and full of books.

Romy found a book about a big tree. On the cover, the word "tree" was printed in green letters. Romy ran her finger under the letters. Her teacher smiled and turned to the first page. "We start here," the teacher said. Romy opened the front cover and read page by page, all the way to the back.

"I want to keep this book forever," Romy said.

The librarian stamped a little card. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back soon, so other kids can read it too."

Romy hugged the book all week. She read it under her blanket. She read it to her stuffed bear. Then she remembered the stamp. She carried the book back to school.

Another girl was waiting at the shelf. She was kind, and she smiled big. "Is that the tree book?" she asked.

Romy put it in her hands. "It starts at the front," said Romy. "Want to read it together?"

activity: Henri is learning something new. What Henri is learning: to draw a map of their bedroom or classroom with a key showing where each thing is.
knowledge_domain: to draw a map of their bedroom or classroom with a key showing where each thing is
story:
Henri wanted to draw a map of his room. He wanted Mom to find his red crayon fast. Mom always said, "Where is it now?"

Henri drew his bed first. He drew it tall, like a door. Then he drew his toy box tall too. Mom looked at the paper. "The bed looks like a wall," Mom did say. "I cannot tell where it is."

Henri sat on the warm floor. He was stuck. Then he climbed up on his bed. He looked down at the toy box. From up high, the box looked flat, like a little square.

"Oh!" said Henri. "A map is how the room looks from up top!"

He drew the bed flat like a rectangle. He drew the rug as a round shape. He put the crayon cup in the middle of the desk. He made a little red dot there.

"Now it is a map," Henri did say. He ran to Mom with the warm paper. "Look in the middle!"

Mom looked at the desk. The red crayon was right there, in the middle of the cup. "Your map works!" said Mom.

Henri smiled big. "A map is from up top. A map is from up top." He drew one more dot for his teddy bear, right by the door.

activity: Through what Jasper sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects.
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jasper ran to the playground with his grandma. The sun made the slide very hot. Jasper touched it with one finger. "Ow! Hot!" he said. He pulled his hand back fast.

Grandma felt the slide too. "The sun heated it up," she said. "We can wait for the shade." They sat on a cool bench under a tree. Jasper saw a tiny dog walk by. The dog sniffed a shiny bottle on the ground. Jasper wanted to touch the bottle. "Not that," said Grandma. "It is not ours. We do not touch it." The dog's owner picked up the bottle and put it in the bin. Jasper clapped.

Then the shade came over the slide. Jasper touched it again. Now it was cool. "The sun moved away, so the slide got cool," he said. He slid down, again and again. Grandma waved from the bench. "Stay where I can see you," she said. Jasper slid one more time and ran back to her. "I stayed close!" he said. Grandma gave him a big hug and a juicy apple.

activity: Through what Mateo sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations.
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Mateo went to the backyard with his bear and his doll. He put them on the grass. "I will play house," he said.

He gave the bear a leaf for a plate. He gave the doll a stick for a spoon. But the doll had no blanket. The wind blew. The doll tipped over.

Mateo heard a sound. It was just his dog, Rex. But Mateo felt worried. "My baby is cold," he said.

Mom sat on the step nearby. "You can fix it," she said.

Mateo ran inside. He got his small red blanket. He wrapped the doll up snug. He counted, "One tuck, two tucks, three tucks."

Then he held the doll close. "The baby cried because she had no blanket," he said. "Now she is warm."

He drew a tiny picture with his pencil for the doll's pretend bed. He put it by her head. Then Mateo hugged his baby tight. "My arms are strong," he said.

Mom smiled. "Time for real lunch," she said.

Mateo carried bear and doll inside, one in each arm. "Home again," he said.

activity: Aiden is learning something new. What Aiden is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Aiden wanted to draw a big sun. But the tablet was dark. He pressed the little button once. Nothing happened. He pressed it again. Still dark.

Then he held the button down. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen grew bright. "It works because I hold it!" said Aiden.

He tapped the blue square, one tap. The drawing app opened. He drew a sun, a tree, and a little dog. He sat with the tablet resting on his knee. His socks were cozy and warm.

When he was done, he did not leave it on the floor. He pressed the button and counted again, "One, two, three." The screen went dark. He set the tablet in its basket by the sofa.

Mom smiled and said, "Thank you, Aiden. Now it will not sink under the toys."

"Dark tablet, bright tablet, all done," said Aiden.

activity: Through what Romy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Romy was at school. The teacher put out three big boxes. One box was for toys. One box was for toy animals. One box was for pretend food. But the boxes were all mixed up.

"I want the bunny," said Romy. She dug in the animal box. Her hand found a car, a banana, and a duck. No bunny. "The bunny is lost," said Romy.

Her friend Tom came over. "Let's sort them," he said. Romy put the car in the toy box. Tom put the banana in the food box. The teacher helped cut an apple for snack time, and Romy put the pretend apple with the food too. Soon every box had the right things.

Then Romy looked in the animal box. There was the bunny! It sat in a little paper nest. "Bunny, you were hiding," said Romy. She gave it a short, soft hug. "I found you."
